**VPN Lab: OpenVPN**

**Objective:**

This lab is designed to give some experience with a virtual private network (VPN).  We will use OpenVPN with symmetric encryption to create a secure connection between 2 systems.  The VPN will increase security in 2 ways: restrict access and encrypt. A new virtual IP tunnel is established between 2 systems that has a restricted pair of IP addresses. Then we will use OpenVPN logs and other Windows artifacts to investigate the VPN process.

**![][image1]**

**Overview:**

This lab needs to be performed with administrative rights, so you will need to use your Win10 VM. Also, we will be performing this lab with a partner in order to create an end-to-end connection for our VPN. Detailed steps are provided in the next section. One system will be designated as the server, and the other as the client.

We will install OpenVPN, and then generate a symmetric secret key. Both of you should generate a secret key so you have the experience, but you must pick one and use just that one for the connection between you. The configuration is reasonably simple using a text editor. When doing so, make sure the correct file extensions are used for configuration files.

The most complicated aspect is that Windows uses a backslash i.e. \\ to separate directories, and the OpenVPN configuration file requires the backslash to be escaped with a \\. Spaces also need to be escaped with a \\ so the path to our configuration file will look something like:

C:\\\\Program\\ Files\\\\OpenVPN\\\\config\\\\username.ovpn

In the configuration, you will define a tunnel, configure the interface with the local VPN IP and the remote VPN IP and provide a path to the configuration file. The client needs to add an additional line to the configuration file designating the LAN IP address of the server so OpenVPN knows who to connect to. 

After the VPN connection is successfully created, we will test it first through pinging each other’s VPN IPs, and then connecting to our partner’s web server through the VPN IPs.

Finally, we will use Wireshark to collect a web transfer on the VPN, and analyze the stream to see what VPN traffic looks like from outside the tunnel.

**Client: Gavin**

**Instructions:**

**Part 1: OpenVPN Installation and Initial Setup** 

* **Both Students** complete this part and Part 2 in their own VM. One student will be the server and the other will be the client, but you should run through the steps together since you will need both configurations and setups in your tech journal.

1. Install [OpenVPN](%20https://swupdate.openvpn.org/community/releases/openvpn-install-2.4.10-I601-Win10.exe) v 2.4.10 (Right click on the installer and run as administrator)

2. Accept defaults until the Choose Components screen. Make sure the following are checked:

   1. OpenVPN Service

   2. TAP Virtual Ethernet Adapter

   3. OpenVPN GUI

![][image2]

3. Complete the installation. When prompted to install the TAP-Windows driver, click Install.

4. We are going to rename the TAP adapter to prevent confusion later: 

   1. Open Network Connections: press Win \+ R **OR** search for run. Use run to open ncpa.cpl

![][image3]

2. Find the new TAP-Windows Adapter that was just installed

   3. Right-Click the adapter and select “Rename”

   4. Name your adapter following this convention:

      **Server:** Firstname-VPN\_Server

      **Client:** Firstname-VPN\_Client

5. Take note of your IP address for later

**Part 2: Key Generation and Distribution**

OpenVPN has a static key mode that uses one symmetric key for both encryption and authentication. Both partner machines need to have a copy of this key. 

Steps to send key:

1. Enable SSH server on server  
   1. Add-WindowsCapability \-Online \-Name OpenSSH.Server\~\~\~\~0.0.1.0  
   2. Start-Service sshd  
   3. Add a firewall rule to allow port 22  
2. Copy key using SCP from client  
   1. scp \-r champuser@10.0.17.24:"C:\\Users\\champuser\\Documents\\key.txt" C:\\Users\\champuser  
1. **Server:** Open a command prompt as an administrator  
   1. Navigate to the OpenVPN Folder: `cd “C:\Program Files\OpenVPN\bin”`  
   2. Generate the Static Key: `openvpn --genkey --secret “C:\Program Files\OpenVPN\config\key.txt”`  
   3. Figure out a way to send your key to the client machine, using any available SECURE method.  
      1. It’s super important that it is secure. Think about it- if you share your symmetric key over an insecure channel and it is intercepted, your VPN tunnel is compromised and essentially useless (**HINT:** SCP or some other secure file transfer protocol).

**Part 3: Configuration and Tunnel Setup**

1. We will be using the private IP space of 10.0.0.0/8 for our VPN tunnel. Coordinate with your partner to pick a random value for X between 0 and 255 to use as a subnet for your connection. 

| Server Tunnel IP | 10.1.X.1 |
| :---- | :---- |
| Client Tunnel IP | 10.1.X.2 |
| Example (X=250) | Server: 10.1.250.1    \|   Client: 10.1.250.2 |

2. **Server:** Create a configuration file for the server in `C:\Program Files\OpenVPN\config\server.ovpn` that looks like this:

```
dev tun
remote (ENTER CLIENT IP)
ifconfig 10.1.X.1 10.1.X.2
secret C:\\Program\ Files\\OpenVPN\\config\\key.txt
--float
# This is my VPN Server Config! -<Server Student's Name>
```

3. **Client:** Get the LAN IP of the server (needed for the remote address) and create the following configuration file in `C:\Program Files\OpenVPN\config\client.ovpn`:

```
dev tun
remote (ENTER SERVER IP)
ifconfig 10.1.X.2 10.1.X.1
secret C:\\Program\ Files\\OpenVPN\\config\\key.txt
--float
# This is my VPN Client Config! -<Client Student's Name>
```

**Part 4: VPN Log Analysis**

OpenVPN writes detailed logs that record every stage of the connection. We’re going to check them while the tunnel is active. 

1. Right-click on the OpenVPN GUI icon and select View Log. This should open a text file. You can also open the log file directly from `C:\Program Files\OpenVPN\log\`   
2. You can also check the Windows Event Viewer: Press Win \+ R, type eventvwr.msc, navigate to Windows Logs, then Application and filter by source “Open VPN”

**Part 5: Other Windows Artifacts**

There are other ways besides logs to see that we set up a VPN tunnel. For each of the Windows tools/locations below, run the associated command, screenshot the results, and reflect on what the results show.

* If you disconnected the VPNs in the last deliverable, reconnect and make sure the right key is back in the config file.

I couldn’t re-connect to Kinder’s VM for this deliverable because his VM was not on when i was completing it and we did not have time to work on this together.

**Deliverable 7:** For each of the Windows tools/locations below, run the associated command, screenshot the results, and reflect on what the results show.

* *Routing Table: `route print`*   
  *![][image20]*

  * *This shows all routes the system knows about. If the VPN was connected that would show up here as another route.*

* *Network Interfaces: `ipconfig /all`*   
  *![][image21]*

  * *This shows all IP configuration on the system. Information about the VPN tunnel also shows up here*

* *Active Connections: `netstat -an`*   
  *![][image22]*

  * *This command shows all active network connections to the device as well as the connection’s port number and the IP address it is going to.*

* *Process Owner: `netstat -b`*   
  *![][image23]*

  * *Shows connections from running programs*

* *Event Viewer: `eventvwr.msc` → `Application`*   
  *![][image24]*

  * *No information was shown about the VPN conncetion*

* *Windows Firewall Log: `WF` → `Monitoring` → `Logging`*
